segments.line: And for one whole day, you are basically a stunt double.
In gym class, a basketball hits you right in the face at full speed.
The whole class gasps.
Your bar loses a tiny sliver.
You blink, and catch the rebound.
After school, you ride your bike off the loading ramp behind the grocery store,
flip once in the air, and land in a hedge.
The bike is ruined. You're not.
Mo is screaming. Mo is also filming.
At the skate park, you go for the biggest ramp.
You overshoot it by twenty feet, bounce off a trash can, and slide across the parking lot on your back like a sled.
A little kid with an ice cream claps. You take a bow.
Then Mo tries a tiny hop off the curb, lands on his knee, and says 'ow' for ten straight minutes.
Same curb. No bar.
By dinnertime, the video has two million views.
Your little sister Ellie watches it nine times in a row. 'Again, ' she says. 'Do it again. '
And here's the part you need to hear. Don't try any of this. You don't have the bar. Nobody does.
Real stunt doubles use crash mats, airbags and months of practice, and they still get hurt sometimes.
You have a green bar and no practice at all. That's the only reason you're fine.
By the evening, your bar is almost empty from all the stunts. You're walking home, waving at Ellie,
and you trip on Mo's skateboard. One tiny trip.
The bar hits zero.
Everything goes black.
You open your eyes in a hospital bed, in a clean gown.
A nurse is staring at you like you just walked through a wall.
Because, technically, you did.
Twenty seconds ago, you weren't in this building.
And at that exact second, every light in the hospital flickers.
